title: Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI Inference

Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI Inference
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Today's AI workloads are rapidly changing: new models are released more often, model architectures are increasingly diverse, and traffic distributions change frequently. The challenge we face at Together AI is continual optimization for these changing workloads. Compiling a deployment into an optimized forward pass is a challenge that is well-suited for agent hill-climbing. Existing systems struggle with continual compilation due to a tradeoff between measurement throughput and fidelity. Many systems use agents to optimize individual kernels from the inference forward pass using offline benchmarks, but timings are low-fidelity because of data-dependent behavior in primitives like mixture-of-experts (MoE). On the other hand, systems use agents to directly optimize end-to-end engines but suffer from slow engine launch times. To address these challenges, we build Together Compiler (TKCC), the first truly continual agent loop designed for AI inference optimization. To address the throughput-fidelity tradeoff, we propose: (1) a Tiered Persistent Engine that decouples engine launch overheads from forward pass computation; (2) a cost model to select the parallelism configurations that seed the optimization process. We also conduct extensive ablations on agent context management and present our insights on deploying TKCC in production. TKCC outperforms highly-optimized hand-written Megakernels on the Llama 1B workhorse workload by up to 1.7x and the best open source engines on the latest frontier models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash) across hardware platforms by up to 2.6x higher TPS on the InferenceX benchmark. TKCC also sets the state-of-the-art performance at batch size 1, with 1111 TPS on M3.1 Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash. Finally, TKCC generalizes beyond frontier language model inference. TKCC serves trillions of tokens across our production fleet.

report.summary: Together AI's TKCC uses a continual agent loop to auto-compile AI inference deployments, beating hand-written Megakernels by up to 1.7x and open-source engines by up to 2.6x.
report.background: AI serving has shifted from a one-time optimization problem to a continuous one: new model architectures ship monthly, mixture-of-experts and other data-dependent primitives behave differently under different traffic, and request mixes drift hour to hour. Conventional inference stacks — hand-tuned kernel libraries, megakernels, and general-purpose serving engines — are optimized against a snapshot of the workload and go stale quickly. Agent-driven optimization promises to close that gap, but existing approaches are caught in a tradeoff: optimizing individual kernels against offline benchmarks gives fast iteration but low-fidelity timings, because MoE routing and similar primitives make kernel speed data-dependent, while optimizing whole engines end-to-end gives faithful numbers but each experiment costs a slow engine launch. Together AI argues this throughput-versus-fidelity dilemma, not raw model capability, is what has blocked truly continual compilation in production.
key_points: The core bottleneck is a throughput/fidelity tradeoff. Kernel-level agents measure fast but inaccurately on data-dependent ops like mixture-of-experts; engine-level agents measure accurately but pay heavy launch costs per experiment, so neither can iterate continuously on live workloads.

TKCC's Tiered Persistent Engine decouples engine startup from forward-pass computation, so the optimizer can keep experimenting without paying launch overhead each time — effectively making high-fidelity end-to-end measurement as cheap as offline benchmarking.

A cost model picks the parallelism configurations (tensor/pipeline/data parallel layouts, batch shapes) that seed each optimization round, narrowing the search space so the agent hill-climbs instead of exploring blindly.

Reported gains: up to 1.7x over highly optimized hand-written Megakernels on Llama 1B, up to 2.6x higher TPS than the best open-source engines on frontier models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash) across hardware, and state-of-the-art batch-size-1 throughput of 1111 and 1205 TPS.

It is not just a benchmark result: TKCC reportedly serves trillions of tokens across Together's production fleet, and the paper includes ablations on agent context management plus practical deployment lessons.
report.impact: If continual compilation works as claimed, it changes where inference performance comes from: instead of waiting for a vendor kernel library or a hand-tuned megakernel, a serving provider can let an agent re-tune the deployment whenever models or traffic shift. That compresses the window between a new architecture shipping and it running efficiently — a real cost for anyone serving frontier models. For developers, it reinforces that agentic search plus reliable measurement loops, not just better kernels, is the frontier; expect more tooling around high-fidelity benchmarking harnesses. For users, the visible effect is cheaper, faster tokens, particularly at batch size 1, the regime that governs interactive chat latency. The caveat: gains depend on a provider's ability to run an optimizer loop, which may widen the gap between large clouds and self-hosters.
report.tools: Watch vLLM and SGLang (the open-source engines TKCC benchmarks against), NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM and its megakernel work, and Triton for writing custom kernels. For the agent side, look at compiler-autotuning projects such as TVM/MLC, OpenXLA, and kernel-optimization benchmarks like KernelBench, plus agent frameworks (DSPy, GEPA-style optimizers) used for search over configurations. The InferenceX benchmark is worth tracking to reproduce TPS comparisons. TKCC itself is described in the arXiv paper rather than released as open source.
